intro: The loud chord is only the first interruption. Haydn takes a tune made from a few notes of C major through four variations, changing its scoring, mode and rhythmic density without losing its outline.
question: What keeps a simple tune recognisable through four variations?

cues.title: A tune to remember
cues.text: The opening theme uses regular phrases, repeated notes and the notes of a C-major chord. Keep its shape in mind: four variations will change the surrounding activity while preserving points of recognition.
cues.evidence: The score gives the theme and four variations. The report places a quiet C-centred passage at the opening; it does not align individual notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The famous interruption
cues.text: The opening theme includes a forceful chord after a very quiet repeated phrase. Listen for the contrast in weight rather than a wrong note: Haydn interrupts a familiar harmonic pattern without abandoning it.
cues.evidence: The score and Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note identify the interruption. Very low recorded level around 0:25–0:35 followed by a change around 0:42 suggests its location; the chord has not been timed by ear.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Decoration around the theme
cues.text: In the first variation, more active decoration surrounds the theme’s harmonic route. Listen for the same regular arrivals beneath the added notes; activity need not mean a new phrase shape.
cues.evidence: The first variation follows the repeated theme. Increased activity around 1:25–1:35 supports a start estimated around 1:24, not a precise instrumental entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Haydn in London
cues.text: Haydn visited London in 1791, writing symphonies for concerts organised by the violinist and impresario Johann Peter Salomon. His last twelve symphonies are known collectively as the London or Salomon symphonies.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil programme note documents the London visit and Salomon’s role: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

cues.title: The minor variation
cues.text: The second variation includes C minor in place of the opening C major. Compare the familiar outline with its changed mode: E♭ in place of E alters the harmonic character without erasing the tune.
cues.evidence: The score specifies the minor-mode variation. A strong level rise and a compatible pitch change around 2:45 suggest its start; the passage continues into other harmonies.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A lighter major-key return
cues.text: The third variation restores C major and a lighter texture. Listen for space around the familiar melody after the more forceful minor-key passage.
cues.evidence: The score places this variation after the minor one. A quiet gap around 4:00 followed by C-centred writing around 4:05–4:10 supports an approximate transition.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognising the phrase endings
cues.text: Through the variations, compare the places where phrases settle rather than only their first notes. The harmonic arrivals can preserve the theme’s outline even when decoration makes the surface less familiar.
cues.evidence: This is a listening suggestion based on the variation design, not an event located at 4:40.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The last variation’s force
cues.text: In the fourth variation, stronger attacks and quicker internal movement enlarge the simple theme. Keep its phrase divisions in mind beneath the added orchestral weight.
cues.evidence: The report shows a marked increase in level and attacks around 5:20, compatible with the score’s fourth variation. Its first bar is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One event, two nicknames
cues.text: English audiences attached the nickname “Surprise”. The German name, “Mit dem Paukenschlag”, means “with the drum stroke”. Both single out the opening interruption in this movement, not the whole four-movement design.
cues.evidence: Both names and their association with the Andante are discussed by Howard: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

cues.title: Weight before the retreat
cues.text: The later variation sustains a stronger sound before the closing withdrawal. Listen for the short phrases organising that weight, and compare them with the quiet opening.
cues.evidence: The highest relative-level windows occur around 6:20–6:35, followed by a pronounced fall around 6:40. The analysis does not establish which players cause the change.

cues.title: The coda looks back
cues.text: In the quiet coda, altered accompanying harmonies change the familiar tune’s setting. This is another kind of surprise: recognition persists while the chords beneath it become less predictable.
cues.evidence: The coda’s reharmonisation is described in Howard’s programme note. The quieter span after the fall around 6:40 suggests its placement, without a bar-level alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet conclusion
cues.text: The movement closes at a lower level than the last variation. Listen to the final phrases and their decay rather than waiting for another large interruption.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls through the closing windows around 7:10–7:15, before the file ends at 7:18. The final release is not precisely timed.

transitions.title: A completed phrase starts moving inside
transitions.how: The repeated second strain closes in C major before the first variation resets the theme’s opening. Haydn keeps the bass’s tonic-and-dominant framework and the two-beat Andante, but adds quicker violin decoration around the recognisable notes. The new activity therefore does not need a modulating bridge: the cadence supplies the hinge, and the tune begins again with a busier surface. Follow the regular phrase arrivals beneath the smaller notes rather than mistaking the ornament for a new melody.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Variation I, 84 s. The report shows increased level and activity around 1:25–1:35; the provisional relations place the repeated second strain at 66.5–84 s and the first variation excerpt at 87–103 s. The score supplies the C-major cadence, violin decoration and retained binary design.

transitions.title: C stays while E falls
transitions.how: The decorated major-key strain finishes, then Haydn restarts the theme in C minor. The tonic and fifth, C and G, remain, but E♭ replaces E♮ and changes the triad’s character. Forceful orchestral attacks make this modal switch much less discreet than the preceding variation’s added notes. The bass still supports recognisable phrase lengths; the melody’s outline remains available inside the more emphatic texture. A new mode and new weight, rather than a long connecting passage, make the boundary audible.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Variation II, 164 s. Relative level rises from −27.8 dB at 2:40 to −10.2 dB at 2:45; E♭ becomes prominent, and a boundary follows at 2:46. The written minor variation establishes the mode change. The relations match its repeated opening from 165 s but do not align its first attack.

transitions.title: The minor variation leaves room for winds
transitions.how: The minor variation’s force contracts towards the dominant, G, and the next statement restores C major. Haydn changes the foreground as well as the third of the chord: flute and oboe take prominent melodic roles above a lighter string foundation. The tune is still organised by the same repeated-note opening and regular cadential points, but a small wind conversation replaces the fuller orchestral declamation. The Andante continues; reduced mass and exposed articulation produce the apparent relaxation.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Variation III, 244 s. The report shows G-centred writing around 3:40–3:50, a low-level gap near 4:00 and a boundary at 4:06. The score supplies the dominant preparation, C-major restoration and wind-led scoring; the recording has no reviewed bar alignment.

transitions.title: The melody acquires orchestral weight
transitions.how: A C-major close becomes the launching point for the fourth variation without a change of key or tempo. Quicker internal notes and stronger full-orchestra attacks enlarge the theme, with brass and timpani adding weight to the string-and-wind texture. The bass’s familiar harmonic route keeps the added activity tied to the original phrase design. What the first variation did through decoration, the last does through mass: the same melodic outline now has to be heard through a much denser surface.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Variation IV, 318 s. Relative level rises from −22.2 dB at 5:15 to −9.9 dB at 5:20, with detected attacks rising to 4.2/s. The score establishes the C-major cadence and fuller, more active final variation; the measurements corroborate the broad change rather than identifying instruments.

transitions.title: A familiar tune finds unfamiliar support
transitions.how: The final variation’s emphatic C-major ending is followed by a sharp withdrawal. Winds recover the simple tune while strings replace its predictable support with more chromatic, changing harmonies. Haydn preserves the recognisable melodic notes but alters what lies underneath them: a note that sounded settled can acquire tension against a new chord. The bass and inner parts now do the surprising, not a sudden timpani blow. This quieter reconsideration still leads back to C major rather than opening a fifth full variation.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Coda, 402 s. The report marks 6:42 after a fall from −9.9 dB at 6:35 to −45.5 dB and no detected attacks at 6:40. Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note describes the wind theme with altered string harmonies. No individual chromatic chord is assigned from the audio estimates. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
